SparseArray vs HashMap  

I can think of multiple reasons why HashMaps with integer keys are significantly better than SparseArrays:  

  1. The Android documentation for a SparseArray states "It is typically slower than a conventional HashMap".  
  2. If you write code utilizing HashMaps rather than SparseArrays your code will function with other implementations of Map and you will be able to employ all of the Java APIs designed for Maps.  
  3. If you write code utilizing HashMaps rather than SparseArrays your code will operate in non-android projects.  
  4. Map overrides equals() and hashCode() while SparseArray does not.  

Yet whenever I attempt to use a HashMap with integer keys in an Android project, IntelliJ informs me I should employ a SparseArray instead. I find this truly difficult to comprehend. Does anyone know any persuasive reasons for utilizing SparseArrays?  

SparseArray can be used to substitute HashMap when the key is a primitive type. There are some variations for different key/value types, even if not all of them are publicly accessible.  

Benefits are:  

  • Allocation-free  
  • No boxing  

Drawbacks:  

  • Generally slower, not recommended for large collections  
  • They won't function in a non-Android project  

HashMap can be substituted by the following:  

SparseArray          <Integer, Object>  
SparseBooleanArray   <Integer, Boolean>  
SparseIntArray       <Integer, Integer>  
SparseLongArray      <Integer, Long>  
LongSparseArray      <Long, Object>  
LongSparseLongArray  <Long, Long>   //this is not a public class                                  
                                    //but can be duplicated from  Android source code  

In terms of memory, here is an illustration of SparseIntArray vs HashMap<Integer, Integer> for 1000 elements:  

SparseIntArray:  

class SparseIntArray {  
    int[] keys;  
    int[] values;  
    int size;  
}  

Class = 12 + 3 * 4 = 24 bytes  
Array = 20 + 1000 * 4 = 4024 bytes  
Total = 8,072 bytes  

HashMap:  

class HashMap<K, V> {  
    Entry<K, V>[] table;  
    Entry<K, V> forNull;  
    int size;  
    int modCount;  
    int threshold;  
    Set<K> keys  
    Set<Entry<K, V>> entries;  
    Collection<V> values;  
}  

Class = 12 + 8 * 4 = 48 bytes  
Entry = 32 + 16 + 16 = 64 bytes  
Array = 20 + 1000 * 64 = 64024 bytes  
Total = 64,136 bytes  

Source: Android Memories by Romain Guy from slide 90.  

The figures above are the quantity of memory (in bytes) allocated on heap by JVM. They may differ depending on the specific JVM used.  

The java.lang.instrument package contains some useful methods for advanced operations like checking the size of an object with getObjectSize(Object objectToSize).  

Extra information is obtainable from the official Oracle documentation.  

Class = 12 bytes + (n instance variables) * 4 bytes  
Array = 20 bytes + (n elements) * (element size)  
Entry = 32 bytes + (1st element size) + (2nd element size)
